summary:
Astro Mission Simulator is a browser-based game where players design, launch and manage a complete space mission. Players choose a destination (Moon, Mars, an asteroid or a satellite) and build a spacecraft by selecting propulsion, fuel tanks, solar panels, communications and scientific instruments. They then plan the trajectory, choose a launch vehicle and allocate resources. Live meters track budget, mass, power, fuel and mission time, and the game explains what to fix before launch.
During the flight, random events such as fuel leaks, communication failures and solar storms force decisions, and the spacecraft design changes the odds of success. A final score, star rating, badges and mission report show how each choice shaped the result.
This addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on experience for students. The game uses NASA’s JPL Horizons API and Solar System Exploration facts, plus real Hubble images.
details:
What it does and how it works
Astro Mission Simulator is a browser game where players take a space mission from concept to results. Players choose a mission (Moon landing, Mars exploration, asteroid exploration or satellite deployment) and build a spacecraft by choosing propulsion, a fuel tank, solar panels, a communications antenna and any mix of scientific instruments (camera, spectrometer, radar, sensors, research lab). They then choose a launch vehicle and a trajectory, and set the fuel load, instrument power share and science days.

Live meters track budget, mass, power, delta-v (the change in speed a spacecraft can achieve) and mission time. They turn red when a limit is broken, and the launch button explains what to fix. Delta-v is calculated with the rocket equation, and solar power drops with distance from the Sun, so Mars gets only about 43% of the sunlight Earth gets. Ion thrusters are very fuel-efficient but need a lot of power and make the trip slower.

After a countdown and an animated launch, the craft flies a transfer to its target. During the flight, random events (fuel leak, equipment malfunction, communication failure, solar storm, asteroid encounter) ask the player to choose a response. Each choice has an outcome chance that depends on the spacecraft design, and the game shows the player that chance. At the end, players get a success percentage, score, star rating, badges, discoveries, remaining resources and a mission report. Players earn XP and ranks, and they can redesign and try again.

NASA data
The game requests the live Mars position from NASA’s JPL Horizons API and falls back to a labelled reference value if the browser blocks the request. Planet, Moon and asteroid facts come from NASA Solar System Exploration. Real Hubble images (Mars, Pillars of Creation, Cygnus) are used in the interface. Eyes on the Solar System inspired the flight view. Costs, masses, mission times and event odds are simplified game values, not real NASA data, and the game says so.

Benefits and intended impact
Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission, so the trade-offs between budget, mass, power, fuel and time stay abstract. This game lets them see why engineers make those compromises, in a few minutes, with nothing to install.

Tools
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), canvas animation, the Web Audio API for sound effects, JPL Horizons API, Google Fonts, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. The code was generated with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic), and our team directed the design and checked the results.

Creativity and factors considered
Instead of random outcomes, every result has a visible reason. We considered accessibility (large text), a beginner-friendly difficulty curve, honest labelling of simulated values, and avoiding NASA logos and branding.
